summary: This informational document defines an information model for the Babel routing protocol: structured data elements an implementation can use to report its current state, and in limited cases accept configuration. It is meant as a base for building data models in different modeling languages, and it covers only parameters useful for running Babel over IPv6.

eli5.summary: A routing program needs a clear list of things you can look at, like a car dashboard. This document lists the dials and switches for the Babel routing program so tools can show and adjust them.

subtitle: A standard structure for reporting and configuring Babel routers.

tldr.problem: The Babel routing protocol lacks a formal information model that tools can use to read the router's state or adjust its settings, making it difficult to build management interfaces or monitoring systems.
tldr.mechanism: This document defines a hierarchical information model with data objects for Babel's configuration, operational state, statistics, and security parameters, written in a notation that can translate into any data modeling language.
tldr.outcome: Network operators and tool builders now have a standard structure for instrumenting Babel routers, whether for NETCONF, YANG data models, or other management frameworks.

facts.label: Primary protocols covered
facts.value: Babel, Babel with MAC, Babel with DTLS

today: RFC 9046 is an Informational RFC published in June 2021. It has not been obsoleted or updated. It serves as the foundation for YANG data models and other management frameworks built to configure and monitor Babel routing instances.

sections.title: What Babel Is and Why It Needs a Model
sections.content:
Babel is a loop-avoiding, distance-vector routing protocol that finds the best paths in a network. It is designed to be simple and to work well in mesh networks with many nodes. Because of its simplicity, most of its information model is focused on reporting state rather than allowing configuration.

Two security mechanisms extend Babel: RFC 8967 adds Message Authentication Code (MAC) authentication, and RFC 8968 adds DTLS for both authentication and encryption. This information model covers all three: plain Babel, Babel with MAC, and Babel with DTLS.

The document provides a foundation for building data models in different languages (like YANG for NETCONF), but does not prescribe any particular one. It covers only Babel over IPv6, as IPv6 is simpler and more widely supported in the devices where Babel is used.
sections.eli5: A router running Babel is like a librarian keeping track of which routes are good. This says what information the librarian tracks and what questions you can ask.

sections.title: The Structure of the Information Model
sections.content:
The information model is organized hierarchically at the top level under a babel-information object. It includes implementation version, enable/disable flags, the router's own ID and sequence number, supported algorithms, and constants like the UDP port and multicast group. Below that are lists for interfaces, routes, MAC key sets, and DTLS certificate sets.

Most parameters are read-only (reporting state). A small set can be configured: enabling/disabling Babel, choosing metric algorithms per interface, managing MAC keys and certificates, and controlling statistics collection. The model uses notation where square brackets mark optional parameters and angle brackets with ranges (like <0..*>) mark lists.
sections.eli5: The model is like a filing cabinet: top level has the big settings, and drawers below hold per-interface details, routes, and security keys.

sections.title: Interface and Neighbor Information
sections.content:
For each interface that runs Babel, the model tracks whether it is enabled, which metric algorithm it uses, whether split-horizon optimization is active, and statistics like the number of Hello packets and updates sent and received. It also lists the neighbors reachable on that interface.

For each neighbor, the model captures its address, transmission cost, expected next sequence numbers for both multicast and unicast Hellos, and the computed link cost. It may also expose Hello history as a binary sequence showing which recent Hellos arrived (useful for diagnosis). The cost values are 16-bit unsigned integers representing link quality.
sections.eli5: Each interface watches its neighbors like a person watching a busy street: counting who walks by, how reliable each path is, and whether messages are getting through.

sections.title: Routes and Security Configuration
sections.content:
The route table in the model shows all known routes: the prefix, prefix length, originating router ID, the neighbor that advertised it, the metric received from that neighbor, the calculated metric, sequence number, and next-hop address. Each route also has a flag for feasibility (whether it can be used per Babel's loop-avoidance rules) and selection (whether it is currently being used for forwarding).

Security is configured through two separate sets: MAC key sets and DTLS certificate sets. Each can be marked to apply automatically to new interfaces. MAC keys must be created with their algorithm (HMAC-SHA256 or BLAKE2s-128) and marked for use in sending or verifying. Key values are write-only (cannot be read back) for security. DTLS certificates store the certificate data, type (X.509 or RawPublicKey), and a private key that is also write-only.
sections.eli5: Routes show where traffic can go. Security settings are like locks on doors: you set them up (but you can never read the keys back out), and you can test them to make sure they work.

sections.title: Statistics and Configuration Notes
sections.content:
The model supports optional statistics collection at the global level and per interface. Global statistics can be reset with a single operation. Per-interface statistics count multicast Hellos, multicast updates, unicast Hellos, unicast updates, and IHU (I Heard You) acknowledgment packets sent, plus total Babel packets received.

Implementations are free to expose parameters as read-only even if the model marks them read-write; this is noted per parameter. For example, an implementation might not allow changing the UDP port after startup, so it might expose that parameter as read-only. The key invariant is that implementations must never return a key value when it is read (only write-only parameters).
sections.eli5: You can count packets in and out to see if the router is healthy. Some settings can be changed, and some can only be looked at, depending on what the vendor decided is safe.
